title: The forgiveness chant
hookLine: a Theravada practice: if I've harmed anyone, I ask forgiveness; if anyone harmed me, I forgive (traditional)

cards: A few short sentences, said slowly, pointing in different directions. If I have harmed anyone, in thought, word or deed, knowingly or unknowingly, I ask their forgiveness.
If anyone has harmed me, knowingly or unknowingly, I forgive them. And in some versions, a further line, turned back toward the speaker: for the ways I have harmed myself, I forgive myself.
Versions of it are taught in meditation halls today, with roots in Theravada Buddhist practice.

teach.h: ASK, FORGIVE, AND TURN IT BACK.
teach.b: Out, in, and back: asking forgiveness, giving it, and turning it toward yourself. The practice doesn't choose between them. It does them together, each time.
That matters, because one is often easier than the others. Some people find asking easy and forgiving hard; for others it's the reverse. Saying them side by side keeps either from hiding.
Then a small phrase that does a lot of work: knowingly or unknowingly. It admits that some of the harm we've done we'll never know about, and that some of the harm done to us was never meant.
It forgives without waiting for a full account of who did what. The roots are older.
In the Pali texts, owning a wrong and having it accepted is part of the path.

In the Digha Nikaya, the Buddha tells a king who has confessed a terrible wrong that seeing a fault as a fault, making amends, and holding back in future is growth in the discipline of the noble ones.
Monks in the Theravada tradition still ask one another's forgiveness, in set words, at certain times.
It isn't meant to be said once and checked off.

Some teachers, the meditation teacher Jack Kornfield among them, teach repeating it many times, over time, and noticing what resists: a face that won't come into focus, a line that sticks in the throat.
That's not failure. It's the part of the work that's still to do.

how: In Theravada communities, monks and lay people ask one another's forgiveness in set words at certain times, and meditation teachers teach a forgiveness practice that asks, gives and turns forgiveness toward oneself, repeated slowly over time.

games.q: you say the first line, and a face comes up you really don't want to ask forgiveness from. what does the practice suggest?
o: notice what resists, and keep saying it slowly.

practice: If you'd like, say the lines slowly, silently or under your breath, with a few breaths between them: if I have harmed anyone, knowingly or unknowingly, I ask their forgiveness; if anyone has harmed me, knowingly or unknowingly, I forgive them, as far as I'm able today.
If it feels right, add a last line toward yourself, and without forcing any of it, notice where the words flow and where they catch.

wordCard.voice: Theravada. The Buddhist tradition whose monks still ask one another's forgiveness, and whose practice gives this chant its roots. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: I ask, I forgive. Out, in, and back, as often as it takes. That's day nine hundred sixty-five.
